Visible-Light Photoredox-Catalyzed Radical-Polar Crossover 1,4-
Hydrofluoromethylation of 1,3-Enynes
Yuejie Sun, Yingjie Pan, Xiaoyun Chen, Huaguang Yu, Ying Han, Qiu Sun, Hong Hou,
and Shaoqun Zhu*
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2024, 26, 10399−10403
 Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
 Article Recommendations *
sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: We report herein a visible-light photoredox-
catalyzed 1,4-hydrofluoromethylation of terminal-alkene-derived
1,3-enynes with sodium fluoromethylsulfinate, providing an
effective protocol to access a diversity of di- and trisubstituted
allenes under mild conditions. The synthetic utility of the present
protocol was demonstrated by a large-scale reaction as well as the
synthetic derivatization of the allene product.
F
luoromethyls, such as CF
3
, CHF
2
, and CH
2
F are
important chemical groups in the field of medicinal
chemistry
1,2
because of their high fat solubility, good metabolic
stability, high electronegativity, and bioavailability. They have a
wide range of applications in bioactive molecules.
3,4
Since the
fluorinated compounds are relatively rare in nature, how to
conveniently, gently, efficiently, and safely introduce fluori-
nated groups into various organic compounds to prepare
special fluorinated compounds is an important research topic
in synthetic chemistry.
5−7
Allenes make up a class of organic molecules with unique
physical and chemical properties. They are not only found as
the key skeleton in numerous natural products and drug
molecules but also serve as an important synthon in the
organic synthesis of bioactive molecules.
8,9
So far, different
strategies, including transition metal activation
10−12
and ionic
1,4-functionalization
13
of 1,3-enyne are well-developed to
prepare allenes.
More recently, a variety of radical methods under thermal
and photochemical reaction conditions have realized the
installation of two functional groups on 1,3-enyne. The
installation of a hydrogen atom onto the allenyl radical species
would lead to hydrofunctionalization product formation, and it
was a challenge due to the rare hydrogen atom donor for this
hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) process (Scheme 1a).
14−18
In the continuation of our photochemical functionalization
project,
19,20
we herein developed a visible-light photoredox-
catalyzed 1,4-hydrofluoromethylation of terminal-alkene-de-
rived 1,3-enynes with sodium fluoromethylsulfinate, providing
effective access to a diversity of di- and trisubstituted allene
derivatives under transition-metal-free conditions (Scheme 1,
b).
The present reaction development was started by testing the
hydrotrifluoromethylation of 1,3-enynes (1a, 0.2 mmol) with
NaSO
2

and THF as the solvent, and Cs

under irradiation with a blue LED at room temperature for 12
h, giving the desired trisubstituted allenes 3a in 60% isolated
yield (entry 1, Table 1). Various solvents, including acetone,

DMF, DMSO, DCE, and MeCN were evaluated next, and
MeCN gave 3a in 88% isolated yield (entries 2−6, Table 1).
Different bases, such as NaO
t
Bu, LiOH, K
3
PO
4
, and DBU
were screened next, and no better result was obtained (entries
7−10, Table 1). The decrease in the amount of 4CzIPN led to
a drop in the yield (entry 11, Table 1). It was surprising to
observe that a decrease of the dosage of radical source 2a did
not affect the reaction, and 1.2 equiv of 2a also gave 3a in 88%
yield (entry 12, Table 1). To our great surprise, when the
mixture solvent of H
2
O and MeCN was tested, the yield of 3a
dropped (entry 13, Table 1).
The visible light, photocatalyst, nitrogen atmosphere, and
inorganic base were essential for this transformation, which
was next confirmed (entries 14−17, Table 1).
With the best reaction conditions established, different
reactions of 1,3-enynes with sodium trifluoromethanesulfinate
2a were carried out to explore the substrate scope, and the
results are listed in Table 2. In general, 1,3-enynes bearing
halogen atoms (Br, Cl, and F) at the para-position of the
phenyl reacted smoothly under the standard conditions and
provided the desired products 3b−3d in 66−98% yields
(entries 2−4, Table 2). Allene with para-trifluoromethyl
substituent 3e was obtained in 95% yield (entry 5, Table 2).
Interestingly, electron-donating groups, such as OMe and
OEt, at the para-position of the phenyl reduced yields, and the
corresponding products 3f and 3g were obtained in 40% and
43% yields, respectively (entries 6 and 7, Table 2). Meanwhile,
the yields were increased with the switch of electron-donor
groups from the para-position to ortho- and meta-positions
(entries 13, 14, and 23, Table 2).
1,3-Enynes bearing different functional groups, such as
phenyl, cyano, ester, and formyl, were all compatible,
delivering the desired products 3h, 3i, 3j, and 3k in good
yields. Halogen atoms at the meta- and ortho-positions of the
benzene ring also delivered the desired allene products 3p−3r
and 3s−3u in moderate to excellent yields. Disubstituted allene
3x was also successfully obtained in 68% yield. The
naphthalene ring containing allene product 3y was obtained
in 87% yield. 1,3-Enyne bearing a structurally complex ester
group on the benzene ring was also well tolerated, giving
desired product 3z in 51% yield (entries 24−26, Table 2).
The scope of fluoromethyl radical sources for the present
transformation was carried out further, and NaSO

1,3-enynes could be effectively applied to these reaction
conditions. As shown in Table 3, electron-donating functional
groups, including methyl and methoxy, as well as electron-
withdrawing functionalities such as halogen (Br, Cl, and F),
trifluoromethyl, and phenyl, were all compatible with the
standard reaction conditions, giving 3aa−3ag in good yields
(entries 1−7, Table 3).
Significantly, this protocol was also compatible with
NaSO
2
CH
2
F. For example, 1,3-enynes bearing trifluoromethyl,
cyano, and halogen substituted on the phenyl ring all gave the
desired products 3ai−3al in good yields (entries 9−12, Table
3). Furthermore, naphthalene-containing 1,3-enynes were
suitable for this 1,4-hydrofluoromethylation protocol, and the
desired products 3ah and 3am were obtained in 70% and 61%
isolated yields, respectively (entries 8 and 13, Table 3).
It should be mentioned that, although some products were
obtained in moderate isolated yields, possible dimerization of
1,3-enynes was completely suppressed, and low reaction
conversion was observed in those cases.
A gram-scale reaction was carried out next, and 5.0 mmol 1c
was successfully subjected to this reaction, giving 3c in 71%
yield (Scheme 2a). The synthetic applicability of this protocol
was further demonstrated by the product derivatization, and
the arylation led to the formation of 1,3-diene 5 in 73% yield
(Scheme 2b).
21
To understand more detailed information on the reaction
mechanism for this 1,4-hydrofluoromethylation protocol,
parallel deuterium radical and deuterium cation experiments
were carried out, and the results suggested that the hydrogen
atom of the sp
2
C−H bond in the allene came from the trace
amount of water rather than the MeCN solvent (Scheme 3a,b).
Based on the above reaction development and previous
reports, a possible reaction mechanism for the present 1,4-
hydrofluoromethylation reaction was proposed in Scheme 3c.
The single electron oxidation of sodium trifluoromethanesul-
fonate by the excited species of the photocatalyst would
generate trifluoromethylsulfonyl radical species I and rapidly
remove SO
2
for formation of the trifluoromethyl radical II.
The addition of trifluoromethyl radical with 1,3-enyne 1a to
generate propargyl radical III, which then rapidly forms allenyl
radical IV via resonance, forms anion species V under the
single electron reduction of PC
−1
. And the protonation of
species V by water would lead to the desired product 3a
formation.
The use of inorganic base, as well as a trace amount of water,
were important for this transformation, probably benefiting
from the suppression of generated sulfuric acid.
In conclusion, we describe a visible-light photoredox-
catalyzed 1,4-hydrofluoromethylation of 1,3-enyne. The use
